justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over longer horizons. For the one-day estimate, I anchored closely to what would have been the prevailing market price, assuming no major overnight catalysts and normal session-to-session continuity. The one-week estimate nudges slightly higher, reflecting a mild bullish bias consistent with broader market trends and typical mean-reversion tendencies after any short-term volatility. The one-month estimate extends that drift further, incorporating a small positive expected return premium while acknowledging that equities historically trend upward over multi-week periods absent recessionary signals.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the fundamental reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the tight range of roughly plus or minus five points captures normal intraday and overnight volatility for a liquid asset. At one week, I widened the interval to plus or minus ten points, accounting for the possibility of macro data releases, Federal Reserve communications, or sector-specific news that could shift sentiment meaningfully. At one month, the twenty-point band on each side reflects the full range of plausible economic developments, earnings surprises, and shifts in risk appetite that can accumulate over four weeks.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside even these wider intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in economic data — such as a sharp jobs miss, a credit event, or escalating geopolitical tensions — could produce a rapid sell-off that breaches the lower bounds. A surprise hawkish pivot from central banks, particularly if inflation data re-accelerates, could also compress valuations quickly. On the upside, a strongly positive earnings season, a sudden de-escalation of geopolitical risk, or a dovish policy surprise could drive prices well above the upper bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon where positive momentum can feed on itself.

It is also worth noting that my intervals are calibrated at a 90% confidence level, meaning I am explicitly acknowledging a 10% probability of outcomes falling outside the stated ranges. Fat-tailed distributions in financial markets mean that extreme moves — flash crashes, sudden liquidity crises, or unexpected macro shocks — occur more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest. Tail events are, by definition, underrepresented in point estimates, and any single unexpected headline could render even the widest intervals insufficient.
